1:
The chapter does not begin where the English says it does. Adam Clarke notes that the Hebrew and all the versions join this verse to the preceding chapter. Charles Ellicott says the same and argues that a new section nevertheless begins here, since what follows is in the second person singular, a form not used before in the book; he finds no obvious connection with what precedes, and suggests the precepts may have been traditionally known as part of the king’s teaching.

Keeping the foot is read three ways. John Gill takes the singular as put for the plural and rules out two senses before offering his own: it does not mean keeping the foot from going in, nor a slow approach, since the motion should be quick and zealous; the allusion, he thinks, is to the pulling off of the shoes commanded on holy ground. John Wesley makes the feet the thoughts and affections, by which men go to God and walk with him. Matthew Henry makes the verse autobiography: having shown the vanity of the world the writer sends us to the temple he had himself built at vast expense, the one work he did not repent of, and does not name it lest he seem to reflect on it with pride. Henry adds that when we are disappointed in the creature we should turn to the Creator, since in the word and in prayer there is a balm for every wound.

The last clause is where the difficulty lies, and Ellicott says outright that the received English is a device. The most natural translation, he holds, would be that they know not how to do evil, that is are incapable of it, which would force us to take the subject as those ready to hear rather than the fools; the received version, he says, exhibits one of the expedients resorted to in order to get a better meaning, and he reports another. Clarke translates the whole verse literally in the same direction, that none of them have knowledge about doing evil, and then explains it from an old paraphrase: they offer gifts for their sins and do not turn from their evil works, because they do not distinguish between good and evil. Wesley keeps the received sense and makes the fools insensible of the great sinfulness of their thoughts.

At the word for being taught Keil and Delitzsch stop to correct a historical assumption. Priests, they say, are probably not in view, since priestly instruction limited itself to information about performing the law already given and to deciding questions of legal practice; the priesthood did not belong to the teaching class in the sense of preaching. Preaching, they add, was never a part of the temple worship at all, and became a part of worship for the first time after the exile, in the synagogue; the preachers of the older covenant were the prophets, preachers by a supernatural divine call and by the immediate impulse of the Spirit. They also report that the rabbis declined to treat this book as apocryphal because it begins and ends with words of the law.

On the dream and the many words Wesley makes a structural argument nobody else makes: the multitude of words here is not prayer but vowing, since the verses that follow are about vows, and the seventh verse, which returns to dreams and words together, reads as a comment on this one, which makes it probable that both are to be understood of vows rather than prayers. Gill and Clarke keep the comparison simple, that as the business of the day breeds confused dreams at night, so a multitude of words betrays the feeble workings of a foolish heart. Clarke sets a passage of devotional verse beside the warning against rashness, counselling that on approaching the altar the strictest guard be set upon the lips.
4:
On the vow they agree and then diverge on how much weight to give it. John Gill points out that a vow is arbitrary: a man is not bound to make one, and until he does the matter stays in his own power. Adam Clarke makes the same point as a caution, that we are under constant obligation to live to God and no vow can make it more so, though there may be cases in which we should bind ourselves to a particular cross. Matthew Henry presses the paying rather than the making, gives a Latin tag that whoever is not inclined today will be more averse tomorrow, and finds two reasons against delay: it affronts God, and it wrongs ourselves, since not vowing would have been an omission while vowing and not paying incurs treachery.

Who the angel is divides them four ways, and Charles Ellicott refutes the majority with three arguments. John Wesley and Clarke both take it for the priest, Wesley because the vow made to God was paid to him as one standing in God’s stead, so that it belonged to him to discharge men from their vows, and Clarke on a prophet who calls the priest a messenger of the Lord of hosts. Henry canvasses three views without settling: the priest, the guardian angel supposed to attend every man, and the Angel of the covenant himself, who cannot be imposed upon. Ellicott rejects the priest outright. Even in the prophet’s passage, he says, there is no trace that the word had become an ordinary name for the priest such as would be intelligible without the context; the priest had no power to dispense with rash vows, the authority given him being of another nature; and the phrase is before the angel, whereas an excuse pleaded to a priest would require say not thou to the priest. He keeps the obvious sense, that the real vow is observed and recorded by a heavenly angel. Clarke reports an old paraphrase making it the cruel angel who will have authority at the last judgment; Gill reports one interpreter taking the flesh to be a man’s children.

On dreams Clarke turns the verse into consolation: one who dreams of evil should give way to no unreasonable fears, since he that fears God need fear nothing else, and an upright soul may say even to the tempter that because it fears God it does not fear him. Henry says that those who heed dreams shall have a multitude of them to fill their heads, and that the way not to be dismayed at signs is to fear God.

The last verse turns on one word. Ellicott says the interpretation depends on the sense given to marvel: some take it of simple surprise, the oppression observed being only part of a gigantic scheme of mutual wrongdoing in which each oppressor is oppressed by his superior, but be not dismayed is preferable, and then the verse answers the gloomy view of the preceding chapter. On the closing clause he confirms a reading of divine rectification by an argument from style, that the author delights in verbal assonances and constantly links words similar in sound, so that the phrase about the high and the higher is meant to suggest the divine name to the ear; he notes in passing the awkwardness of explaining the plural as a king and the favourites who govern him. Henry takes the higher ones for both the angels and the courts above, the council to which the princes of provinces are accountable. Keil and Delitzsch render the clause as one high one watching over another with others above both, and defend an unparalleled phrase for the robbery of right and justice against a critic who thought it impossible. Clarke observes that such oppression was frequent under all governments, especially in provinces far from the seat of power.
9:
The ninth verse is the crux of the chapter, and no two settle it alike. Keil and Delitzsch take it as praise of a patriarchal government founded on agriculture, whose king takes pride not in conquest but in the peaceful welfare of his people, and render it that the advantage of a country consists in a king given to the arable land. They dispose of two rival renderings by name: one making him a king set over the land, answered from idiom since the phrase for making a king is different; and another making him served by its citizens, answered by asking whether a population could be worse designated than by the word for a field. Charles Ellicott reports their rendering as that of many eminent interpreters and calls it hard to clear of irrelevance; he keeps the received English and connects the verse forward, the paragraph being meant to mitigate the sight of riches got by oppression, since riches add little to the happiness of those who hold them. John Gill offers two further senses, that the excellency of the earth is God’s rule above all its oppressors, or the preference of country over city for having fewer tumults.

Two of them read the verse politically. Adam Clarke makes it a joining of head and feet: the peasant is protected by the king as executor of the laws, and the king depends on the peasant, the wealth of the nation being the fruit of the labourer’s toil. Matthew Henry draws a duty from the same fact, that those who have abundance must remember the fruits are for all and look on themselves as stewards bound to give to those who need; dainty meats and soft clothing, he adds, are only for some, but the fruit of the earth is for all, and the king would be quite starved without it. John Wesley makes the verse a return, after some interruption, to the vanity of riches, one evidence being that the poor labourer enjoys the fruits of the earth as well as the greatest monarch.

On the insatiableness of money they reach for maxims. Clarke quotes a Latin line that the love of money increases as money itself increases; Keil and Delitzsch quote another that the covetous man is always in want. Gill reaches for the horse leech that cries Give, give, and observes that a man cannot eat his bags of silver. Henry supplies the best formulation, that natural desires are at rest when what is desired is obtained but corrupt desires are not, so that nature is content with little, grace with less, and lust with nothing; and if a man be hungry, ingots of silver satisfy no better than clods of clay.

At the increase of goods Keil and Delitzsch distinguish the man in view from a miser who feeds on looking at his money in a chest; this man is covetous, and as his property grows so does the number he must maintain. Henry puts it as a proverb, the more meat the more mouths, and observes that an empty speculation is all the difference between the owner and those who share with him. Gill cites a figure from Xenophon to the same effect. On the labourer’s sleep Keil and Delitzsch note that the Greek renders the word as slave, as if the original were another, and answer that sound sleep is the reward of earnest labour, so that since there are idle servants as well as active masters there is no privilege to servants; they prefer husbandman; Gill reports one interpreter making him a tiller of the ground, another a servant of the Lord. Henry explains both halves physiologically: the labourer’s weariness rocks him asleep and his labour gives him a good digestion, while the rich man’s sleep is broken by care, by what he has eaten, and perhaps by a consciousness of guilt.
13:
Both of those who enumerate do it in the same style. Adam Clarke lists four ways in which riches are kept to their owner’s hurt: improper use that costs him his health; an unfortunate partnership; the desire of the robber, who may take his life as well as his goods; or a profligate son who spends the whole. He adds that he has seen this again and again. Matthew Henry divides the same ground three ways: their riches do them hurt, making them proud and in love with the world; they do hurt with their riches, having the means of oppressing others; and they sustain hurt by them, since they would not be envied or robbed if they were not rich, and it is the fat beast that is led first to the slaughter.

Two of them trace the language to the same source. Keil and Delitzsch say the author has the patriarch of Uz in mind at the thirteenth verse, and that the fifteenth is a reminiscence of his words. Charles Ellicott finds the same clear use of that book, and notes that this passage is in turn used by a later writer. Henry expands the picture: as friends helped him with swaddling clothes when he came naked into the world, so when he goes out they help him with grave clothes, and that is all; we are born with our hands griping, he says, but die with them extended. On the labour for the wind he observes that those who labour for the world labour for what has more sound than substance; men will see it when at death they find the profit of their labour gone like the wind, they know not whither.

The seventeenth verse carries a variant, and the three who notice it do three different things. Clarke reports that instead of the received he eateth, several manuscripts read he walketh, and adopts it: he walks in darkness, has no evidence of salvation, and no ray of light penetrates the gloom. Keil and Delitzsch report the same variant and two more, one giving in mourning and another in darkness, noting which versions support each; but they keep the received text on the authority of the Targum, an old version and the Masora, and separately refuse a critic’s attempt to take the days as the object of the verb, since one may say in Hebrew as in Latin that a man consumes the days of his life but not that he eats them. Ellicott, elsewhere the readiest of them to emend, passes the whole thing by in one sentence, leaving unnoticed some variations of translation which do not materially affect the sense.

John Gill supplies the most concrete reading of the darkness. He takes it generally for a miserable manner of living, coarse bread and a poor cottage; but he reports an interpreter who takes it literally of the night, to which such a man defers eating so as to lose no working time, so that his poor fare may not be seen, and so that others may not eat with him. Clarke keeps to the fear, the possibility of being deprived filling the heart with anguish, and quotes a poet on a man counting on long years of pleasure and quite unfurnished for the world to come. John Wesley explains the wrath: when he falls sick and foresees death he is filled with rage at being cut off before accomplishing his designs and having to leave the wealth in which all his hopes lie. Henry adds that he is angry at the providence of God, at his sickness and at all about him, which doubles his affliction, where a good man lessens his by patience.
18:
All of them treat the passage as a return rather than an advance. Charles Ellicott notes in a single line that the Preacher is led back to the conclusion at which he had arrived. Keil and Delitzsch make the same observation from the opening word: with behold he here returns to it, for from the observations just spoken of, as from others, no other result befell him. Matthew Henry supplies the inference — from the vanity of riches hoarded up, that the best course is to use well what we have and to do good with it.

Two of them divide the commendation in two. John Wesley glosses it briefly: good or comfortable to a man’s self, and comely or amiable in the eye of other men. Henry says the same at length — it is well, and it looks well; there is duty and decency in it — and then fixes the limits on both sides. We are not to indulge the appetites of the flesh nor to take present pleasures for our portion; but neither are we to starve ourselves through covetousness, nor through excessive care and grief, nor to kill ourselves with labour and then leave others to enjoy the good of it. Nor is the calling itself to be done as a drudgery.

On the portion the accounts run parallel and then part. Adam Clarke holds that God gives every man the necessaries of life in the course of his providence and wills that he should thankfully use them, and that earthly blessings are as truly the portion of his body as the salvation of God is the portion of his soul. Wesley draws the same line in a phrase: the portion is of worldly goods, and he hath a better portion in heaven. Henry parcels out the whole — God must have his part, the poor theirs, our families theirs, and this is ours. John Gill takes an inventory instead, counting estate personal and real, goods movable and immovable, all of them the gift of God by whatever means acquired. Keil and Delitzsch add what the grammar carries: the sentence is built without proper sequence and cannot be rendered so into English, but its force is that cheerful enjoyment is not made possible by the possession of earthly treasures, being a special gift added thereto.

The last verse divides them. Gill gives the plain sense, that he will not think life long and tedious nor distress himself with the troubles he has met; but he then reports an interpreter he approves, whose accentuation yields the opposite — if he has not much, he remembers the days of his life, calling to mind how he has been supplied hitherto and trusting that he shall not want. Keil and Delitzsch keep the plain sense, that over this enjoyment he forgets the frailty and the darkened side of life; they mark one explanation incorrect, endorse a second in its revised form, and note that an ancient version read the verb as occupies rather than answers, which would have required another form of the word, while Jerome helped it out by reading a different noun. Wesley glosses each phrase in turn: remember, so as to disquiet himself; the days, meaning the troubles; answereth, his desires, in giving him solid joy and comfort. Henry has him remember them as waters that pass away, since a cheerful spirit makes the yoke of our employments easy and the burden of our afflictions light. Clarke sums it up: such a man passes through things temporal so as not to lose those that are eternal. Ellicott alone records that the usual explanation does not satisfy him, and that he cannot suggest a better.
